name: Thymosin Beta-4

b.x: In two Phase II ulcer trials, topical thymosin beta-4 sped healing by almost a month in the patients whose wounds did close ([PMID 23050815](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23050815/)). Complete healing in the pressure ulcer trial, though, was no higher than placebo: 14.8% vs 16.7% by day 84 (NCT00382174). Thymosin beta-4 (Tb4, CAS 77591-33-4) is a 43-amino-acid protein with a molecular weight of approximately 4,921 Da. Tb4 is the most abundant actin-sequestering protein in human cells. It locks G-actin monomers in place, which controls when and where cells migrate, divide, and differentiate. That single mechanism feeds into wound closure, blood vessel formation, and progenitor cell activation. The N-terminal Ac-SDKP tetrapeptide (released by enzymatic cleavage) adds a second layer: anti-fibrotic and cardioprotective signaling that reduces scar tissue and protects cardiomyocytes from oxidative damage. In practice, the community uses Tb4 primarily for athletic soft tissue injury recovery (tendons, ligaments, muscles) and post-surgical wound healing. The typical loading protocol runs 2 to 2.5 mg subcutaneous, two to three times per week for 6 weeks, followed by weekly maintenance. Stacking with BPC-157 is the dominant community approach; the two cover different healing phases through separate signaling pathways. Research status as of October 2026: two independent Phase I safety trials found IV Tb4 well tolerated. One went up to 1,260 mg [1]; the other topped out at 25 mcg/kg [2]. Phase II data exists for wound healing and dry eye. Only eye drops (RGN-259) reached Phase III; no injected Tb4 trial has. In SEER-1, a neurotrophic keratopathy trial, 6 of 10 treated patients healed fully after 4 weeks vs 1 of 8 on placebo, short of significance (p=0.0656, [PMID 36613994](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36613994/)). A 2025 cardiac RCT (n=96 STEMI patients) found significant infarct reduction in the early-treatment subgroup (n=43) but missed significance in the full cohort. No FDA approval exists for any indication. Tb4 is not on the 503A bulks list, and its TB-500 fragment is listed as withdrawn on FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026).

Tb4 sequesters G-actin monomers. That sounds abstract until you consider what actin polymerization controls: cell migration, proliferation, differentiation, and wound closure. By regulating the pool of available G-actin, Tb4 is a master switch for tissue repair timing. The central LKKTETQ domain (amino acids 17 to 23, shared with the TB-500 fragment) binds actin directly. This promotes cell motility and angiogenesis at injury sites. Blood vessel formation accelerates nutrient and oxygen delivery to damaged tissue. Full-length Tb4 carries something the fragment does not. The N-terminal Ac-SDKP tetrapeptide, released by enzymatic cleavage, provides distinct anti-fibrotic signaling. It attenuates inflammatory macrophage infiltration, reduces fibroblast overactivity, and protects cardiomyocytes from oxidative stress. ACE normally degrades Ac-SDKP; patients on ACE inhibitors may see raised Ac-SDKP levels and stronger anti-fibrotic effects (a clinically relevant interaction). Tb4 also activates integrin-linked kinase (ILK). This drives cardiac progenitor cell activation and epicardial cell migration. After tissue injury, platelets and macrophages release Tb4 to protect surrounding cells from secondary damage. A 2025 study tied this repair to ErbB2 in mice; in its 96-patient STEMI trial, only the group dosed within 8 hours of PCI had significantly smaller infarcts (Zhang et al., Cardiovasc Res 2025, [PMID 41229390](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41229390/)).
Thymosin beta-4 benefits center on tissue repair, anti-fibrotic activity, and systemic healing support across multiple organ systems.

Wound healing acceleration in Phase II data: topical Tb4 sped healing by almost a month in patients whose ulcers closed ([PMID 23050815](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23050815/)), though complete pressure ulcer healing matched placebo (14.8% vs 16.7% at day 84, NCT00382174).
Cardioprotective Ac-SDKP domain that TB-500 (7aa fragment) does not contain; this tetrapeptide reduces fibrosis and protects cardiomyocytes from oxidative injury [3] [4].
Community users consistently report faster return to training after tendon, ligament, and muscle injuries within 2 to 4 weeks of loading, across an estimated 200 to 500 Reddit threads.
Reduced scar tissue formation at chronic injury sites through direct anti-fibrotic signaling via macrophage modulation and fibroblast suppression.
Neuroprotective properties observed in preclinical traumatic brain injury models, with Tb4 reducing inflammation and promoting neural cell survival [5].

Systemic anti-inflammatory effect reported by users within the first 1 to 2 weeks of loading; the body's own platelets and macrophages release Tb4 after tissue damage, and exogenous dosing amplifies this endogenous response.
Partially Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 14 key studies · Research only
Phase I safety established in two independent healthy volunteer trials (IV, up to 1,260 mg in, and up to 25 mcg/kg in) [1] [2].

Dosing studied: Phase I (IV): 42–1,260 mg as single and 14 daily doses (PMID 20536472) and 0.05–25 mcg/kg (PMID 34346165), safety/PK only, not community-applicable. Clinical trial wound/ophthalmic: topical gel or eye drops, not SC injection. Community-extrapolated SC: 2–5 mg/week (loading), 2–2.5 mg/week (maintenance).

Phase II efficacy data: wound healing (pressure ulcers: complete healing 14.8% vs 16.7% placebo by day 84, NCT00382174; faster closure in healers, [PMID 23050815](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23050815/)), dry eye, venous ulcers. Phase III trials tested RGN-259 eye drops. ARISE-2 and ARISE-3 in dry eye completed but missed their registered primary endpoints (NCT02974907, NCT03937882). SEER-1 in neurotrophic keratopathy stopped early after 18 patients (registry: business decision; paper: slow recruitment). It missed its primary endpoint: 6 of 10 healed vs 1 of 8 on placebo (p=0.0656; NCT02600429, PMC9820614). 2025 cardiac RCT (n=96 STEMI) showed significant infarct reduction in early-treatment subgroup (n=43) but not full cohort. No FDA approval for any indication as of October 2026.
Key Study

Cardiovascular Research 2025, Vol 121(17): Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of rhTβ4 in 96 STEMI patients post-PCI. Early-treatment subgroup (rhTβ4 within 8h post-PCI, n=43): significant infarct area reduction vs placebo at 90 days; ErbB2-dependent mechanism confirmed in parallel murine I/R model. Full cohort (n=96): non-significant. Most clinically significant human cardiac efficacy signal to date. PMID 41229390
Limitations

No FDA approval for any indication, and no Phase III trial has tested injected Tβ4. Phase III ophthalmic trials missed or inconclusive on primary endpoints. 2025 cardiac RCT full cohort non-significant; early-treatment subgroup result requires confirmation. Long-term safety data absent. Tβ4 is not on the 503A bulks list; its TB-500 fragment is listed as withdrawn on FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026). Full-length 43aa vs 7aa TB-500 fragment frequently conflated in community reports, confounding evidence interpretation. SC pharmacokinetics formally uncharacterized: all PK data is IV-derived.
Community Experience
Strongly endorsed for athletic soft tissue injury (tendons, ligaments, muscles) and post-surgical wound healing.
Community dosing: 4–8 mg/week loading (2–4 mg per injection, 2–3x/week) for 4–8 weeks; 2–4 mg/week maintenance (1–2x/week)

Most community discussion conflates full-length 43aa Tβ4 with TB-500 (7aa fragment): protocols labeled "TB-500" may or may not reflect full-length product. Full-length Tβ4 is considered by advanced users to have broader benefit (cardiac, anti-fibrotic, immunomodulatory) but is harder to source and verify.
What users report (6)
Faster return to training after tendon, ligament, and muscle injuries: commonly noted within 2–4 weeks of loading
Reduced localized pain and inflammation at injury site
Improved range of motion and joint pliability during loading phase
Wound healing acceleration (overlaps with Phase II clinical data for pressure ulcers)
Systemic anti-inflammatory effect felt within first 1–2 weeks of loading
Reduced scar tissue formation at chronic injury sites
Common issues (6)
Cost: full-length 43aa more expensive than TB-500 fragment (~$8–16/mg vs ~$5–8/mg); typical 8-week cycle (20 mg) costs $90–$320 at research prices
Labeling confusion: must verify "43aa" on label; many products labeled "TB-500" contain the 7aa fragment without distinguishing it from full-length
Reduced availability due to FDA enforcement actions (2024–2026)
No community consensus on dosing frequency (daily vs 2–3x/week): creates protocol confusion
Flu-like symptoms and fatigue in first 1–2 weeks of loading phase
COA with mass spectrometry needed to confirm identity but rarely checked by users: mislabeled products common

Science evidence is concentrated in ophthalmic (Phase III), wound healing (Phase II), and cardiac (Phase II). Community uses Tβ4 primarily for athletic soft tissue injury: mechanistically plausible extrapolation from wound healing evidence but not directly studied in RCT format. Both science and community converge on a healing/regenerative use case. Dosing frequency diverges: clinical trials used structured loading regimens; community standard is 2–3x/week SC. Doses are broadly comparable when expressed as weekly totals.
Community Community dosing consensus from peptide research communities

First thing: make sure your product is actually 43 amino acids. The community conflates Tb4 with TB-500 constantly, and product labels don't help. If your COA doesn't show a molecular weight near 4,921 Da on mass spectrometry, you probably have the 7aa fragment (843 Da). HPLC purity alone can't tell the difference. Reconstitution math for common vial sizes. A 5 mg vial plus 1 mL bacteriostatic water gives you 5 mg/mL (5,000 mcg/mL). On a U-100 insulin syringe, each unit equals 50 mcg. So 2,000 mcg (a standard loading dose) is 40 units; 2,500 mcg is 50 units; 1,500 mcg is 30 units. For a 2 mg vial plus 1 mL BAC water, you get 2 mg/mL; 750 mcg (beginner tier) is 37.5 units. Store reconstituted vials refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees C and use within 2 to 3 weeks. Lyophilized powder keeps for up to 24 months refrigerated. Use bacteriostatic water, not sterile saline (saline shortens shelf life after reconstitution). The short half-life (about 2 hours IV) is why daily or frequent dosing makes sense. But the dominant community convention is 2 to 3 times per week at higher doses; either approach can be justified, and the 2 to 3x/week schedule is more practical.
Cycling Protocol

Loading phase: full dose 3x/week for 6-12 weeks. Then maintenance: half dose 1-2x/week. All protocols run 8-12 weeks. Standard community and integrative medicine protocols recommend 6 weeks off after each cycle for receptor sensitivity recovery.
Thymosin Beta-4 Cycle

Community and integrative medicine protocols recommend 6 weeks off after each cycle based on receptor sensitivity recovery: sustained Tβ4 exposure may downregulate progenitor cell responsiveness and actin-binding pathway signaling. The 6-week off period also provides a window to objectively assess healing progress before reinitiation, and reduces theoretical risk of continuous angiogenic promotion in the context of any undetected occult malignancy. The short IV half-life (~2h) ensures rapid plasma clearance, but downstream cellular effects (progenitor activation, angiogenic signaling) may persist significantly longer.
No further injury healing progress at week 8 despite continued dosing: diminishing returns indicate cycle completion
Increasing injection site nodule formation despite site rotation: suggests local inflammatory sensitization
Return of fatigue or flu-like symptoms mid-cycle after initial resolution: possible immune response to the peptide
Injury fully resolved: no indication for continued loading; transition to off-cycle
Wash hands thoroughly and wipe vial tops with an alcohol swab.

Alternative Routes
Subcutaneous injection

Community: 2–5 mg SC per injection, 2–3x/week. No formal human bioavailability comparison vs IV. All PK data (PMID 20536472) is entirely IV-derived. SC absorption rate and peak plasma levels are unknown in humans.

Abdomen or thigh. Systemic effect: no need to inject near injury site. Use 29–31G needle. Rotate sites at every injection. Reconstitute with bacteriostatic water (not sterile saline: shorter shelf life with saline).
Intravenous (IV)

Phase I trials used 42–1,260 mg IV as single and 14 daily doses (PMID 20536472, far above any community SC dose) and 0.05–25 mcg/kg IV (PMID 34346165). Registered phase 2 STEMI trials: 0.25 to 2.0 mcg/kg IV once daily for 7 days after PCI (NCT05485818, NCT05984134). Half-life 0.95–2.1h (dose-dependent) characterized only via IV route.
Used in clinical trials for controlled PK characterization and cardiac applications. SC remains the only practical community route.
Ophthalmic drops (0.1%)

RGN-259 protocol: 0.1% Tβ4 ophthalmic drops 5x/day × 4 weeks (Phase III SEER-1 and SEER-2 design). Topical ophthalmic route does not provide systemic healing effects. Engineered tandem tTβ4 (IOVS Nov 2025, PMC12636994) shows 7-fold improved corneal epithelial migration vs standard monomer: next-generation formulation not yet in clinical trial.

RGN-259 by RegeneRx Biopharmaceuticals, not FDA-approved as of October 2026. Not available as a consumer product. ARISE dry eye Phase III series: inconclusive. SEER-2, a Phase 3 trial in neurotrophic keratopathy (NCT05555589), is listed as recruiting.
Works With
BPC-157

The dominant healing stack. BPC-157 acts through nitric oxide signaling and growth hormone receptor modulation; Tβ4 acts through actin dynamics and progenitor cell activation: complementary mechanisms covering different healing phases. BPC-157 targets early inflammatory resolution; Tβ4 drives angiogenesis and cellular migration.
BPC-157 250–500 mcg SC daily + Tβ4 2–2.5 mg SC 2x/week (loading 6 weeks) → Tβ4 2 mg 1x/week (maintenance 4–6 weeks). 6 weeks off after cycle.
GHK-Cu

Copper peptide adds anti-inflammatory signaling, collagen synthesis promotion, and angiogenesis support. Commonly added for wound healing or skin repair to complement Tβ4 anti-fibrotic and cellular migration effects.
GHK-Cu 1–2 mg topical or SC daily alongside Tβ4 loading protocol for wound or skin healing goals.
KPV
Short tripeptide with anti-inflammatory properties. Community users add KPV for additional systemic or gut anti-inflammatory coverage alongside Tβ4, particularly for systemic inflammation goals.
KPV 500 mcg–1 mg SC or oral daily alongside Tβ4 protocol.
Avoid
Bevacizumab / Anti-VEGF biologics (ranibizumab, aflibercept)

Directly opposes Tβ4 mechanism of action. Anti-VEGF therapies block the angiogenesis that Tβ4 actively promotes. Concurrent use is mechanistically contradictory and may negate therapeutic effect of both agents.
Warfarin / Anticoagulants (heparin, DOACs)

Tβ4 promotes angiogenesis and may increase bleeding risk at healing sites. Clinical significance uncertain but additive bleeding risk is a real concern, particularly post-surgical or with active wound healing.
Systemic corticosteroids

Corticosteroids suppress the inflammatory cascade that Tβ4 modulates. Concurrent systemic corticosteroid use may blunt Tβ4 healing response by suppressing the immune signaling Tβ4 requires to drive tissue repair.
Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate)

Tβ4 modulates immune cell migration and macrophage activity. Effect of concurrent immunosuppressive therapy on Tβ4 activity is unknown. Use with caution in transplant patients or those on chronic immunosuppression.
Generic / Research

Research-grade 43aa full-length Tβ4 (April 2026): ~$78–$80/5mg (~$16/mg, 99%+ purity with MS confirmation), with discounted listings as low as $45/10mg ($4.50/mg, >98%). Typical 8-week cycle at ~20mg total = $90–$320 at current research prices. TB-500 (7aa fragment) for comparison: ~$5–8/mg.
Compounded

Not on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23); the TB-500 fragment is listed as withdrawn on FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026). TB4-Frag oral spray is a distinct product (oral fragment, not injectable full-length).
Pricing updated 2026-04-09

The most serious concern with Tb4 is its relationship to cancer biology. Tb4 promotes angiogenesis, cell migration, and proliferation. All three processes can support tumor growth and vascularization. Some in vitro studies show Tb4 upregulation in tumor tissue; others show anti-tumor effects. Phase I and II trials found no cancer-promoting signals at tested doses, but long-term human data does not exist. Active cancer or personal cancer history is a firm contraindication. Published safety data comes from two Phase I trials in healthy volunteers. The IV study [1] tested single doses from 42 mg to 1,260 mg and reported no dose-limiting toxicities. Adverse events were infrequent and rated mild to moderate. The Chinese Phase I study [2] confirmed tolerability in a separate population. Total human safety database for injectable Tb4 is small (fewer than 200 participants across all trials combined). Community-reported side effects during loading phase (weeks 1 to 2): Fatigue and flu-like symptoms are the most commonly flagged issue. Users describe 3 to 7 days of mild malaise during the initial loading period. This typically resolves by week 2 to 3. If fatigue persists beyond two weeks or fever exceeds 100.4 degrees F, reducing dose or stopping is appropriate. Headache occurs at moderate frequency. Mild nausea and lightheadedness are less common but reported. Injection site reactions include redness, mild swelling, and nodule formation. Nodules develop from repeated injection at the same site. Rotating locations at every injection and using 29 to 31 gauge needles reduces this risk. Occasional mild water retention has been noted during maintenance phases. Contraindications: active cancer or cancer history (angiogenic risk), pregnancy or breastfeeding (no safety data), active systemic infections (immune modulation concern), known hypersensitivity to Tb4, and concurrent anti-VEGF therapy (directly opposes mechanism). Drug interactions worth knowing: anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) may carry additive bleeding risk at healing sites. ACE inhibitors block Ac-SDKP degradation and may potentiate anti-fibrotic effects. Anti-VEGF biologics (bevacizumab, ranibizumab) are contraindicated. Immunosuppressants have unknown interaction profiles with Tb4 immune modulation. Stop dosing and consult a physician if you develop persistent fever, skin rash, hives, signs of anaphylaxis, or any new suspicious mass or lump.
Common Issues & Solutions

No healing response by week 3: Verify product is full-length 43aa (not 7aa TB-500 fragment): check the COA for mass spectrometry confirming molecular weight ~4,921 Da. The 7aa fragment (~843 Da) may provide less benefit for non-angiogenic healing goals.

Fatigue and flu-like symptoms in week 1–2: Expected during loading phase from immune modulation and angiogenic signaling initiation. Typically resolves by week 2–3. If persistent beyond 2 weeks or fever >100.4°F develops, reduce dose or discontinue.

Injection site nodules forming: Rotate injection sites at every injection (do not reuse same location within same week). Use 29–31G needle and inject slowly over 10+ seconds. Nodules indicate local SC trauma from site overuse.

Product uncertainty (post-2026 enforcement): FDA enforcement actions shrank the market. Only a batch-specific third-party COA confirms what a vial holds. If label says "TB-500" without "43aa," assume it is the 7aa fragment.

ACE inhibitor interaction: If taking an ACE inhibitor, ACE normally degrades Tβ4's Ac-SDKP fragment. ACE inhibition elevates Ac-SDKP levels and may potentiate anti-fibrotic effects: potentially beneficial but uncharacterized at community doses. Inform prescribing physician.

Anti-VEGF therapies (bevacizumab, ranibizumab): directly opposes Tb4 mechanism of action; concurrent use is contraindicated
Immunosuppressants: Tb4 modulates immune cell migration and macrophage activity; effect on immunosuppressive therapy is unknown

Warfarin / Anticoagulants (heparin, DOACs)

Tβ4 modulates immune cell migration and macrophage activity. Effect of concurrent immunosuppressive therapy on Tβ4 activity is unknown. Use with caution in transplant patients or those on chronic immunosuppression.
Thymosin Beta-4: Product Quality high risk

Three compounding risk vectors: 1) Mislabeling: 7aa TB-500 fragment (~843 Da) frequently sold as full-length 43aa Tβ4 (~4,921 Da), or vice versa; amino acid count must be confirmed by mass spectrometry, not HPLC alone. 2) Regulatory squeeze: FDA enforcement has severely contracted the market. 3) No compounding route: Tβ4 is not on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23).
A third-party COA needs mass spectrometry (MS): HPLC purity alone cannot distinguish 43aa from 7aa fragment
Confirm molecular weight on COA: 43aa full-length Tβ4 = ~4,921 Da; TB-500 7aa fragment = ~843 Da
Reject any product labeled only "TB-500" without "43aa" stated explicitly: default assumption is 7aa fragment
Research-grade pricing for verified 43aa: ~$8–16/mg; pricing significantly below this range is a red flag for mislabeled 7aa product

Thymosin beta-4 is classified as a research chemical in the United States. It does not hold FDA approval for any therapeutic indication as of October 2026. Thymosin beta-4 is not on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) and appears in none of FDA's 503A categories (May 14, 2026). FDA's Category 2 entry was its LKKTETQ fragment (TB-500), which FDA's page lists as withdrawn (current as of April 22, 2026). Research-grade Tb4 is still sold online, but only a batch-specific third-party COA with mass spectrometry confirms product identity. Tb4 is prohibited by WADA for competitive athletes. This content is for educational and research purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any research peptide.

faqs.q: Is TB-500 the same as Thymosin Beta-4?
faqs.a: No. TB-500 is a synthetic 7-amino-acid fragment (LKKTETQ, residues 17-23) of full-length thymosin beta-4 (43 amino acids). They share the central actin-binding domain, but full-length TB4 has additional functional regions including the Ac-SDKP cardioprotective domain. Products are frequently mislabeled: "TB-500 (43aa)" is actually full-length TB4. Always verify the amino acid count on a third-party COA.

faqs.q: Does full-length Thymosin Beta-4 work better than TB-500 for injury recovery?
faqs.a: Mechanistically yes: full-length retains the Ac-SDKP domain responsible for anti-fibrotic and cardioprotective effects that TB-500 lacks. But the smaller TB-500 fragment may penetrate tissue more effectively due to its lower molecular weight (843 Da vs 4,921 Da). Most published research used full-length TB4, making TB-500's evidence base largely inferred. For pure soft tissue healing, community reports are comparable; for cardiac or fibrotic issues, full-length has better evidence.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stack Thymosin Beta-4 with BPC-157?
faqs.a: Yes: it's the most common healing stack in the peptide community and makes mechanistic sense. BPC-157 works through nitric oxide signaling and growth hormone receptor modulation; TB4 works through actin dynamics and progenitor cell activation. They address different healing phases. One caution: both promote angiogenesis, so if you have cancer history or active malignancy, monitor for additive effects.

faqs.q: Does Thymosin Beta-4 promote tumor growth?
faqs.a: It's a real theoretical concern worth taking seriously. TB4 promotes cell migration, blood vessel formation, and proliferation: all processes that can support tumor growth. Research is mixed: some in-vitro studies show TB4 upregulation in tumors; others show anti-tumor effects. Phase I and II trials found no cancer-promoting signals at tested doses, but long-term human data is absent. The contraindication for active cancer or cancer history is appropriate.

faqs.q: Why does the protocol say "daily" when most sources recommend 2-3x per week?
faqs.a: The "daily" framing reflects the short 2-hour IV half-life: daily dosing maintains more consistent plasma levels. But the dominant community and clinical convention is 2-5 mg administered 2-3x per week (loading), then 1x weekly (maintenance). Both can be justified. Daily lower-dose gives smoother receptor exposure; 2-3x weekly higher-dose is more practical and better-supported by clinical trial designs.

faqs.q: What is the recommended Thymosin Beta-4 dosage?
faqs.a: Thymosin Beta-4 dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 750 mcg 3x/week, moderate users at 1.5 mg 2-3x/week, and aggressive protocols use 3 mg 3x/week.

faqs.q: How do you reconstitute Thymosin Beta-4?
faqs.a: Thymosin Beta-4 typically comes in 2mg or 5mg vials. Add 1mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Thymosin Beta-4?
faqs.a: The half-life of Thymosin Beta-4 is ~2 hours (IV). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: In two Phase II ulcer trials, topical thymosin beta-4 sped healing by almost a month in patients whose wounds closed, though complete healing in the pressure ulcer trial matched placebo. Full-length Tb4 is a 43-amino-acid protein and the body's primary G-actin sequestering molecule, controlling cell migration, tissue repair, and angiogenesis through multiple functional domains.
